title: Voice and Video AI
description: Explore AI tools for audio transcription, voice generation, video processing, and the practical — and ethical — implications of each.

data.text: Audio and video AI tools have quietly become some of the most practically useful AI capabilities available today. From instant meeting transcription to turning a podcast into a blog post, this category delivers real-world time savings most people are not yet using.

This category is also where AI capability and ethical risk overlap most visibly. Voice synthesis that saves hours of narration work is built on the same technology that enables voice fraud. Video generation that creates compelling B-roll in minutes is related to the deepfake pipeline. Understanding both sides — what these tools can do for you and what they make possible in bad hands — is necessary context for using them responsibly.
The voice and video AI landscape

data.text: Transcription: turning speech to text

AI transcription has become remarkably accurate — often exceeding 95% word-level accuracy on clear audio. Modern tools add speaker identification, timestamps, and searchable transcripts automatically, turning hours of audio into structured, searchable text in minutes.

The underlying technology powering most transcription tools is OpenAI's Whisper model — an open-source speech recognition system trained on 680,000 hours of multilingual audio. Whisper handles over 100 languages, manages strong accents well, and maintains high accuracy even with background noise. Because it is open-source, Whisper runs locally on your machine (via tools like MacWhisper or the command line) as well as powering many commercial products. Knowing this helps you understand why transcription quality across different tools is often similar — many are using the same underlying model.
What affects transcription accuracy
Transcription accuracy is not a fixed property — it varies significantly with audio quality. Understanding the factors helps you get better results and know when to review output carefully.

rows: Large effect — budget microphones and phone mics introduce noise
Use a dedicated USB microphone for recordings that will be transcribed
Significant — traffic, HVAC, and crowd noise reduce accuracy
Record in a quiet room; use noise-reduction apps like Krisp or NVIDIA RTX Voice
Major degradation — models struggle with crosstalk
Encourage turn-taking; use directional mics for each speaker if possible
Moderate — Whisper handles accents better than older models
Speak clearly; review output for misheard words in technical sections
Moderate — medical, legal, and technical jargon is often mis-transcribed
Manually review and correct proper nouns, acronyms, and domain terms
Small — most tools handle MP3, WAV, M4A equally well
Prefer WAV for highest quality when storage is not a concern

data.text: High-value transcription workflows

data.title: Podcast to blog post workflow
data.content:
1. Record podcast episode
2. Transcribe with Whisper or Otter.ai
3. Paste transcript into Claude or ChatGPT
4. Prompt: "This is a podcast transcript. Create a structured blog post (~800 words) covering the main points. Use the speaker's voice and examples. Add an intro and conclusion. Do not invent facts not in the transcript."
5. Edit the draft — add your analysis and links

Time saved: 2-3 hours of manual note-taking and writing per episode

data.title: Meeting to action items workflow
data.content:
1. Record meeting via Fireflies, Otter, or built-in Zoom/Teams transcription
2. Feed transcript to AI
3. Prompt: "From this meeting transcript extract: (1) key decisions made with rationale, (2) action items as [Owner: Task by Date], (3) open questions not resolved. Keep under 300 words."

Time saved: 30-45 minutes of manual meeting notes per session

data.title: Interview research workflow
data.content:
For journalists, researchers, and UX practitioners who conduct interviews:

1. Record the interview (with participant consent) using Riverside.fm or your recorder app
2. Transcribe with Whisper or Otter.ai — enable speaker diarisation to label each speaker automatically
3. Paste the transcript into your AI chat tool
4. Prompt: "This is a research interview transcript. Identify: (1) the top 3 themes that emerge across the participant's answers, (2) direct quotes that best illustrate each theme, (3) any contradictions or surprising positions the participant expressed."

This converts a 60-minute interview into analysis-ready structured notes in under 10 minutes. The AI identifies patterns across a long transcript that would take a human researcher 30-60 minutes to manually code.

data.text: Voice synthesis: text to speech

AI voice synthesis has crossed the threshold of believability. Tools like ElevenLabs generate speech indistinguishable from a real person. The practical uses are widespread — narration, accessibility, explainer videos — and the ethical risks are equally real.

Modern voice synthesis works using neural text-to-speech (TTS) models trained on thousands of hours of human speech. Unlike older robotic TTS systems, current models learn prosody — the natural rhythm, stress, and intonation patterns of human speech — producing output that sounds genuinely conversational rather than mechanically even. Voice cloning extends this by fine-tuning a model on a small sample of a specific person's voice (as little as 30 seconds in some tools), allowing the system to generate new speech in that person's voice from any text input.
Practical voice synthesis use cases

The most useful applications of voice synthesis in everyday work are narration for video content (explainers, tutorials, product demos) without recording yourself, accessibility features (converting written content to audio for audiences who prefer listening or have visual impairments), rapid prototyping of podcast or audio product concepts, and reading long documents aloud while multitasking. The combination of a language model for writing and a TTS model for voice turns a text workflow into an audio workflow with minimal added effort.

data.title: Written article to audio version
data.content:
A newsletter writer wants to offer an audio version of each issue without recording themselves:

1. Write the newsletter as normal
2. Paste the text into ElevenLabs — select a consistent voice persona across issues
3. Adjust speaking rate slightly slower than default for easier listening
4. Export as MP3 and embed in the newsletter

Total added time per issue: under 5 minutes. Readers who prefer audio or are commuting get a frictionless way to consume the content. The voice is consistent across issues, which builds familiarity over time.

data.text: Video AI: what is useful today

rows: Edit video by editing the transcript
Delete filler words by deleting text
Turn a 1-hour recording into 5 highlight clips automatically
Short B-roll clips and concept visualization

data.text: Text-to-video: what it can and cannot do yet

Text-to-video generation (tools like Runway Gen-3, Sora, and Kling) captures a lot of attention but has important limitations to understand before building it into a workflow. The technology is genuinely impressive for short atmospheric clips — landscape B-roll, abstract motion, product reveal cutaways — and continues to improve rapidly. But it is still unreliable for anything requiring consistent characters across shots, coherent narrative sequences, legible text, or realistic human movement in close-up.

rows: Short atmospheric B-roll (landscapes, cityscapes, abstract motion)
Concept visualization for presentations and pitches
Complex narrative sequences with cause and effect
Realistic close-up human movement and expressions
Legible text appearing within the video
Generating visual options quickly for creative direction
Long clips (most tools cap at 4–10 seconds reliably)

data.text: The most practical positioning for text-to-video today is as a fast B-roll replacement: instead of licensing stock footage or shooting filler footage yourself, generate a few atmospheric clips to break up a talking-head or screenshare video. At that use case, the current quality is more than sufficient and the time savings are real.
Transcript-based video editing with Descript

Descript deserves special attention as one of the most genuinely workflow-changing video tools available. Its core innovation is transcript-based editing: import your video, Descript transcribes it automatically, and from that point the video timeline is driven by the text. To remove a section, you delete the words in the transcript. To remove every 'um' and 'uh' in a recording, you run the automatic filler word removal — Descript finds them all in the transcript and deletes the corresponding video segments in one click. To reorder sections, you cut and paste text.

data.title: 30-minute tutorial video editing workflow with Descript
data.content:
Traditional workflow: 3-4 hours editing a 30-minute raw recording

Descript workflow:
1. Import raw video → Descript auto-transcribes in ~5 minutes
2. Run 'remove filler words' → all ums, uhs, and long pauses removed automatically
3. Read transcript, highlight awkward sections, delete text → video cuts automatically
4. Add captions in one click from the existing transcript
5. Export finished video

Total editing time: 30-45 minutes for a 30-minute video
Time saved: 2-3 hours per video

The mental model shift — editing text rather than timeline — is what makes this fast. Most people read and edit text far faster than they scrub through video timelines.

data.text: Voice and video AI ethics

data.title: Deepfakes and non-consensual use
data.text: Voice cloning and video generation can be misused to create fake audio or video of real people without consent. This technology is used in fraud, disinformation, and social manipulation. When evaluating media: verify the source independently, check with reverse image/audio search tools, and be especially skeptical of surprising or sensational audio/video of public figures.

The same ElevenLabs voice cloning capability that lets a podcaster produce consistent narration can be used to clone a CEO's voice for a vishing (voice phishing) attack. The same Runway video generation that helps a filmmaker create B-roll can generate a convincing fake video of a politician saying something they never said. These are not hypothetical risks — voice fraud incidents using AI-cloned voices have already been documented in financial fraud cases. Understanding the technology means understanding both its creative potential and its misuse surface.

Detecting AI-generated audio and video is an active research area. Current tell-tale signs of AI voice include unnatural breath patterns, perfectly even cadence, slight metallic resonance, and the absence of the small vocal variations (creaks, catches, micro-pauses) that characterise real human speech. For video, look for inconsistent lighting on the face, unnatural blinking patterns, slightly soft edges around the head, and background distortion. These artifacts are decreasing with each model generation — which is precisely why source verification matters more than content inspection.

data.title: Ethical use principles:
items: Only clone or replicate a voice with explicit, documented consent from that person
Label AI-generated audio and video clearly in any published content
Do not use AI-generated voices to impersonate real people for deception
Check your platform terms — most video platforms prohibit undisclosed AI avatars for monetized content

data.text: How to critically evaluate audio and video you encounter

As synthetic media becomes more convincing, the most reliable verification strategy shifts from inspecting the content to investigating the source. The following questions apply regardless of how convincing a piece of audio or video appears.

rows: Who is sharing this, and what is their track record?
Authentic media is typically shared by established journalists, verified accounts, or primary sources — not anonymous accounts sharing a single sensational clip
Is there corroborating coverage from independent outlets?
Real events that produce newsworthy audio or video are almost always covered by multiple independent sources
Does the original source material exist?
Authentic audio or video of a public figure is usually traceable to an original press conference, interview, or official recording
Has a detection tool been applied?
Tools like Hive Moderation, AI or Not, and ElevenLabs' own detector can flag synthetic audio — imperfect but a useful additional signal
Does the content match what you know about this person's positions and manner of speaking?
Not a reliable test alone — but significant divergence from known positions warrants extra scepticism

data.title: Voice and video AI essentials
points: Transcription: Whisper (free, accurate, local), Otter.ai (live meetings), Fireflies (auto-join + archive)
Best workflows: podcast to blog post, meeting to action items, interview to themed analysis
Audio quality matters: microphone, noise, and crosstalk are the top accuracy factors
Voice synthesis: ElevenLabs and OpenAI TTS are best-in-class for realistic speech
Practical TTS uses: narration, accessibility, audio newsletter versions
Video AI most useful today: auto-captions, transcript-based editing (Descript), clip generation (Opus Clip)
Text-to-video is reliable for B-roll and atmosphere — not yet for consistent characters or narrative
Always label AI-generated audio/video and only clone voices with explicit consent
Verify suspicious media by source, not just by how convincing it sounds or looks
